edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), Ad Scapulam, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Non te terremus, qui nec timemus: sed velim, ut omnes salvos facere possimus, monendo μὴ θεομαχεῖν. Potes et officio jurisdictionis tuae fungi, et humanitatis meminisse, vel quia et vos sub gladio estis. Quid enim amplius tibi mandatur, quam nocentes confessos damnare, negantes autem ad tormenta revocare? Videtis ergo quomodo ipsi vos contra mandata faciatis, ut confessos negare cogatis. Adeo confitemini innocentes esse nos, quos damnare statim ex confessione non vultis. Si autem contenditis ad elidendos nos, jam ergo innocentiam expugnatis. Quanti autem praesides, et constantiores et crudeliores, dissimulaverunt ab hujusmodi caussis! ut Cincius Severus, qui Thystri ipse dedit remedium, quomodo responderent christiani, ut dimitti possent; ut Vespronius Candidus, qui christianum quasi tumultuosum civibus suis satisfacere dimisit; ut Asper, qui modice vexatum hominem, et statim dejectum, nec sacrificium compulit facere, ante professus inter advocatos et adsessores, dolere se incidisse in hanc caussam. Pudens etiam missum ad se christianum in elogio concussione ejus intellecta dimisit, scisso eodem elogio, sine accusatore negans se auditurum hominem secundum mandatum. Haec omnia tibi et de officio suggeri possunt, et ab eisdem advocatis, qui ipsi beneficia habent Christianorum, licet acclament, quae volunt. Nam et cujusdam notarius cum a daemone praecipitaretur, liberatus est: et quorumdam propinquus et puerulus, et quanti honesti viri (de vulgaribus enim non dicimus) aut a daemoniis aut valetudinibus remediati sunt! Ipse etiam Severus pater Antonini, Christianorum memor fuit. Nam et Proculum christianum qui Torpacion cognominabatur, Euhodeae procuratorem, qui eum per oleum aliquando curaverat, requisivit, et in palatio suo habuit usque ad mortem ejus: quem et Antoninus optime noverat lacte christiano educatus. Sed et clarissimas foeminas et clarissimos viros Severus sciens hujus sectae esse, non modo non laesit, verum et testimonio exornavit, et populo furenti in nos palam restitit. Marcus quoque Aurelius in Germanica expeditione christianorum militum orationibus ad Deum factis, imbres in siti illa impetravit. Quando non geniculationibus et jejunationibus nostris etiam siccitates sunt depulsae? Tunc et populus acclamans Deo deorum, qui solus potens, in Jovis nomine Deo nostro testimonium reddidit. Praeter haec depositum non abnegamus, matrimonium nullius adulteramus, pupillos pie tractamus, indigentibus refrigeramus, nulli malum pro malo reddimus. Viderint, qui sectam mentiuntur, quos et ipsi recusamus. Quis denique de nobis alio nomine queritur? quod aliud negotium patitur christianus, nisi suae sectae? quam incestam, quam crudelem, tanto tempore nemo probavit. Pro tanta innocentia, pro tanta probitate, pro justitia, pro pudicitia, pro fide, pro veritate, pro Deo vivo, cremamur; quod nec sacrilegi, nec hostes publici, verum nec tot majestatis rei pati solent. Nam et nunc a praeside legionis, et a praeside Mauritaniae vexatur hoc nomen, sed gladio tenus, sicut et a primordio mandatum est animadverti in hujusmodi. Sed majora certamina, majora sequuntur praemia.
pass_a_gloss: We do not frighten you, who do not fear; but I wish that we may be able to make all safe by warning not to fight against God; you are able to perform the duty of your jurisdiction and to remember humanity, or because you also are under the sword; for what else is commanded to you, than to condemn the guilty who have confessed, but to recall those who deny to torments? You see therefore how you yourselves act against the commands, so that you force those who have confessed to deny; so much do you confess that we are innocent, whom you do not want to condemn immediately upon confession; but if you contend to destroy us, then you attack innocence; how many presidents, and more constant and more cruel, have dissimulated in cases of this kind; as Cincius Severus, who himself gave a remedy to the Thystrians, how Christians might respond, so that they might be dismissed; as Vespronius Candidus, who dismissed a Christian, who was satisfying his citizens as if tumultuous; as Asper, who moderately harassed a man, and immediately released him, and did not compel him to make a sacrifice, having previously professed among advocates and assessors, that he was grieved to have fallen into this case; Pudens also dismissed a Christian sent to him, having understood the concussion of the same eloquence, with the eloquence torn, without an accuser denying that he would hear the man according to the command; all these things can be suggested to you, both from duty and from the same advocates, who themselves have benefits from Christians, although they may cry out what they want; for even a certain notary, when he was being thrown down by a demon, was freed; and relatives and a little boy, and how many honest men (for we do not speak of common people), either from demons or from illnesses, have been remedied; even Severus, the father of Antoninus, was mindful of Christians; for he also sought out Proculus, a Christian who was surnamed Torpacion, a procurator of Euhodea, who had once cured him with oil, and had him in his palace until his death, whom also Antoninus knew very well, having been educated on Christian milk; but even very famous women and very famous men, Severus, knowing them to be of this sect, not only did not harm, but also adorned with testimony, and openly resisted the raging people against us; also Marcus Aurelius, in the German expedition, having made prayers to God by Christian soldiers, obtained rains in that drought; when have our genuflections and fasts not even driven away droughts? then also the people, crying out to the God of gods, who alone is powerful, in the name of Jupiter, gave testimony to our God; besides these things, we do not deny a deposit, we do not adulterate anyone's marriage, we treat orphans piously, we refresh the needy, we return no evil for evil to anyone; let those see, who lie about our sect, whom we also reject; who finally complains about us under another name? what other business does a Christian suffer, except that of his own sect? which, so incestuous, so cruel, no one has proven for so long a time; for such great innocence, for such great integrity, for justice, for chastity, for faith, for truth, for the living God, we are burned; which not sacrilegious people, not public enemies, but not even those who have committed so many crimes against majesty, are accustomed to suffer; for even now the name is harassed by the president of the legion, and by the president of Mauritania, but only with the sword, as it was commanded from the beginning to take notice of such people; but greater struggles, greater rewards follow

pass_b_english:
We aren't trying to frighten you — you don't scare — but we do want to bring everyone to safety by warning you not to fight against God. You can fulfill the duties of your office and still remember your humanity; after all, you too live under the sword. What exactly does your commission order beyond this: condemn the guilty when they confess, but send those who deny it to the rack? So look at what you're doing: you're acting against your own orders, forcing confessors to recant. That amounts to an admission that we're innocent, since you refuse to condemn us the moment we confess. And if you press on to destroy us, you're attacking innocence itself.

Plenty of governors — sterner and more brutal than you — have quietly looked the other way in cases like this. Cincius Severus once coached the Thystrians on how Christians should answer so they could be released. Vespronius Candidus let a Christian go, telling his citizens the man was a public disturbance. Asper roughed a man up a little, then released him at once and refused to force a sacrifice, having already told his legal advisers and assessors how sick it made him to be handed a case like this. Pudens dismissed a Christian sent to him once he saw the power of the man's eloquence; he tore up the charge sheet and, with no accuser left, refused to hear the case on the governor's orders. All of this can be cited to you both as a matter of official duty and by the very advocates who owe their own careers to Christians, no matter what they shout in court.

Even a notary, thrown down by a demon, was set free; so were relatives, a little boy, and any number of respectable men — I'm not talking about commoners — healed either of demons or of diseases. The emperor Severus, father of Antoninus, honored Christians. He tracked down Proculus, a Christian surnamed Torpacion and procurator of Euhodea, who had once cured him with oil, and kept him in his palace until the man died — a man Antoninus knew well, since he was raised on Christian milk. Severus also knew that many high‑ranking women and men belonged to this sect; he not only refused to harm them but decorated them with honors and publicly shielded them from a mob raging against us. Marcus Aurelius, on his German campaign, got rain for his parched army after Christian soldiers prayed to God. When have our kneeling and fasting ever failed to break a drought? At that moment the crowds themselves, crying out to the God of gods who alone holds power, invoked Jupiter's name and bore witness to our God.

On top of all this, we don't embezzle deposits, we don't violate anyone's marriage, we raise orphans with care, we relieve the needy, we never return evil for evil. Let the liars who slander our sect look to themselves — we disown them. Who brings any other charge against us? What crime does a Christian commit except belonging to this sect? No one has ever proved it incestuous or cruel, not in all this time. For such innocence, such integrity, for justice, chastity, faith, truth, and the living God, we are burned alive — a fate that even sacrilegious criminals, public enemies, and traitors guilty of the worst high treason don't usually suffer. Right now the name is being hunted by the legion's commander and the governor of Mauritania, but only by the sword, just as it was ordered from the beginning that such people be punished. Yet greater struggles bring greater rewards.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex legal and historical arguments of the Latin text. Pass A provides a literal rendering, while Pass B provides a fluent English version that maintains the nuances of the Latin (e.g., 'majestatis rei' as 'high treason', 'scisso eodem elogio' as 'tore up the charge sheet'). All historical names and specific examples (Cincius Severus, Vespronius Candidus, Asper, Pudens, etc.) are correctly preserved.
